vignette:
Eleanor keeps her small apartment immaculate. Everything has its place: the worn social work textbooks on the shelf, the porcelain teacups arranged by size, the single afghan folded neatly over the arm of the chair. Order feels like safety. For most of her life, it was enough. Now, at eighty, the silence of her orderly rooms has become a resonating chamber for the past.

It began over fifty years ago, when she was a young woman just starting her career. She met Robert at a university function. He was a history professor, charismatic and brilliant, with a way of making her feel like the only person in the world. The first year was a whirlwind of intellectual debates, jazz clubs, and dizzying affection. She was finishing her MSW, learning about family systems and cycles of violence in a detached, academic way. She never imagined those concepts would soon become the architecture of her own life.

The first time he hit her, it was an open-handed slap that spun her head and left a ringing in her ears. It came after she’d stayed late at the library to finish a paper. He was terrified, he’d said, that something had happened to her. He was so sorry, his love for her was just so immense, so overwhelming, it sometimes came out wrong. She was a social worker in training; she understood complicated emotions. She believed him.

Over the next four years, the apologies grew shorter and the violence more inventive. He never left marks on her face, always choosing places her clothes would cover. He was a historian; he was methodical. He would often lecture her as he hurt her, his voice a calm, academic drone explaining her failures as a partner while his hands did their work. The most terrifying moments were the quiet ones that followed, when he would hold her and cry, promising it was the last time. In her work at a family services agency, she was counseling women in situations identical to her own. She would listen to their stories, map out safety plans, and connect them with resources, all while a deep, corrosive shame settled in her bones. She was a fraud, helping others escape a prison she returned to every night.

She finally left after he broke her wrist, an injury she explained away at the hospital as a fall down the stairs. The lie was so practiced, so easy, that it terrified her more than the break itself. She packed a single bag while he was at the university and never went back.

For decades, work was her salvation. She poured everything into her career, becoming a respected supervisor, a fierce advocate for her clients. She built a life of quiet solitude, with friends kept at a safe, professional distance. She never dated again. The idea of letting a man into her home, of that specific vulnerability, was unthinkable. She managed the memories by staying busy, by transmuting her pain into helping others.

Retirement stripped all of that away. Without the daily demands of her job, the structure that held the past at bay crumbled. Now, a car door slamming in the street below sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through her, her heart hammering against her ribs. She can’t watch old movies anymore; the sight of a man raising his voice to a woman on screen makes her feel a cold dread, the phantom smell of Robert’s whiskey-laced breath filling her nostrils.

Sleep offers no escape. She often wakes up tangled in her sheets, the echo of his calm, lecturing voice in her ears, her body braced for an impact that never comes. In the daytime, she sits in her quiet, orderly apartment, tracing the raised line of the old scar on her wrist. She feels suspended, a ghost in her own life, forever tethered to that young woman on the cold kitchen floor, wondering how she, who knew all the right answers for everyone else, got it so terribly wrong for herself.
